# Incident Report: NetSupport RAT Infection — DESKTOP-TEYQ2NR

**Evidence source:** `2026-02-28-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (only artifact present in evidence directory; no separate IDS/Suricata export was supplied)
**Capture window:** 2026-02-28 23:55:06 to 2026-03-01 04:16:35 (capture-local timezone, ~4h21m)

## 1. Victim Host

| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| IPv4 address | 10.2.28.88 |
| MAC address | 00:19:d1:b2:4d:ad |
| Windows hostname | DESKTOP-TEYQ2NR |
| NetBIOS workgroup / AD domain | EASYAS123 / easyas123.tech |
| Logged-in Windows user | **brolf** (EASYAS123\brolf, Kerberos CNameString and realm EASYAS123.TECH confirm this account performed AD authentication from .88) |

Confirmed via DHCP (option 12 hostname = DESKTOP-TEYQ2NR, requested IP 10.2.28.88, chaddr 00:19:d1:b2:4d:ad), NBNS name registrations for DESKTOP-TEYQ2NR and EASYAS123 from 10.2.28.88, and Kerberos traffic between 10.2.28.88 and the domain controller (10.2.28.2, EASYAS123-DC.easyas123.tech, MAC 14:b3:1f:2d:ce:69).

## 2. Malware Family

**NetSupport RAT** — malicious abuse of the legitimate NetSupport Manager remote-control client/gateway protocol.

**Attribution basis: signature-confirmed (protocol-level), not merely behavioral.** No Suricata/IDS alert file was included in the evidence set, so this is not confirmed via a rule hit; however the traffic itself contains the literal, distinctive NetSupport Manager wire protocol, which is functionally as strong as a signature match:

- HTTP `POST /fakeurl.htm` — the known NetSupport gateway check-in endpoint
- `User-Agent: NetSupport Manager/1.3` on every request
- Decoded POST bodies are the raw NetSupport client-gateway protocol grammar:
  - `CMD=POLL\nINFO=1\nACK=1\n` (frame 2638, and repeated)
  - `CMD=ENCD\nES=1\nDATA=<encrypted hex blob>\n` (frame 2639 and all subsequent POSTs)
- The session is a single, persistent TCP connection (10.2.28.88:51912 ↔ 45.131.214.85:443) that stays open for the remainder of the capture (~4.3 hours), carrying 264 `POST /fakeurl.htm` request/response pairs — a beacon/poll loop, not a one-off web request.
- The connection uses **plaintext HTTP on TCP/443** (no TLS ClientHello observed on this stream) — a common NetSupport RAT trait used to blend with normal HTTPS egress while avoiding real TLS overhead.

## 3. Indicators of Compromise

**Command-and-control endpoint:**
- IP:port — `45.131.214.85:443`
- Domain — `vadusa.xyz` (resolved by DESKTOP-TEYQ2NR to 45.131.214.85 at DNS query, single A-record answer, no other resolutions observed)
- URL — `http://45.131.214.85/fakeurl.htm` (beacon/poll endpoint, 264 POSTs observed)

**Files / hashes:** No executable, script, or other payload transfer was observed anywhere in this capture (checked all HTTP objects, all requests with executable-type extensions, and Content-Disposition headers — none present). The captured traffic is exclusively the post-infection C2 beacon channel; the initial dropper/loader is not present in this pcap, so no file name or SHA256 can be grounded in the evidence.

**Possible lure/initial-access correlation (not conclusively provable from this pcap):** DESKTOP-TEYQ2NR opened a TLS session to `www.fmcsa.dot.gov` (23.64.147.24) at relative time ~44.49s into the capture. The DNS lookup for `vadusa.xyz` occurred ~0.3s later (~44.77s), and the NetSupport RAT beacon connection to 45.131.214.85 began ~0.4s after that (~44.89s) — all within the same one-second window, while the fmcsa.dot.gov TLS session was still active. Because that session is TLS-encrypted, its page content cannot be inspected, so this is reported only as a **timing correlation**, not a confirmed delivery mechanism.

**All other external destinations contacted by the host** (Microsoft telemetry/update/login endpoints, Bing/MSN, Adobe ARM/DTM, Windows Update CDN, NVIDIA GFE, Google Update) were reviewed and are consistent with normal enterprise workstation background traffic — no additional indicators found among them.

## Summary

DESKTOP-TEYQ2NR (10.2.28.88, MAC 00:19:d1:b2:4d:ad), logged on as EASYAS123\brolf, is actively beaconing to a NetSupport RAT command-and-control server at `vadusa.xyz` (45.131.214.85:443) via a persistent HTTP POST loop to `/fakeurl.htm`, running for the entire remainder of the capture. This is remote-access-trojan C2 traffic requiring host isolation and full incident response; no dropped-file hash could be recovered from this capture alone.
